title: Med Spa Discount Policy: Stacking, Staff Pricing and Approvals (October 2026)
summary: Write a med spa discount policy that sets stacking rules, staff pricing, birthday offers and who can approve an override, so each checkout gets one answer.
body_markdown:
## What a Med Spa Discount Policy Has to Cover


A med spa discount policy has to answer five questions in writing: which discounts exist, which can combine, who is eligible, who can override them, and when they end. Everything else is wording.


Published examples show how much variation sits inside those five answers. One university med spa runs monthly specials and states that[other discounts cannot be combined with them](https://www.odu.edu/node/1042105) . An Arizona clinic sells memberships that include[10% off fillers and other non-surgical treatments](https://naturalresultsaz.com/?p=272) . Both are defensible choices. A clinic that does neither on paper ends up making the call at the counter, one patient at a time.


Keep the policy to a page, give it an owner, and date it. If your offers sit on top of recurring plans, read it alongside your[membership pricing and retention](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-membership-pricing-retention) rules, because member discounts are the offer most likely to collide with everything else.


## Stacking Rules: Which Discounts Can Combine


The safest stacking rule is one discount per ticket, with a short list of named exceptions. Each offer is priced as if it stands alone, so a 15% promotion on top of a 20% member rate is a 32% reduction nobody planned.


Build a table once and post it where staff can see it. Here is a starting point for a clinic with memberships, seasonal promotions and staff pricing:


Offer Can combine with Applies to Excluded


Membership benefit Nothing, by default Services on the member's plan Products, sale items


Seasonal promotion Nothing Named services only Injectables priced per unit


Staff rate Nothing Services and retail Anything already discounted


Birthday credit A membership benefit, if you choose Any service, one use Gift card purchases


Referral reward Nothing Next visit Package purchases


The "excluded" column does the real work. Per-unit neurotoxin is the clearest case, because the product cost does not move when the price does. Our guide to[Botox unit pricing](https://decodahealth.com/blog/botox-unit-pricing-med-spa) shows the margin math that makes a flat percentage off injectables so costly.


Commissions need the same clarity. If a provider is paid on revenue, say whether the number is the list price or what the patient paid, which the[injector commission structure](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-injector-commission-structure) guide walks through.


## Employee Discount Policy: Eligibility, Caps and Exclusions


A staff discount needs four limits: who qualifies, what it covers, how much it takes off, and how often it can be used. Without them it turns into an open-ended perk that touches your most expensive products.


Generic templates are a reasonable skeleton. The[Workable employee discount template](https://trainual.com/template/employee-discount-policy) covers eligibility, a cap and exclusions, and bars use on items already on sale or alongside other offers. It is written for retail, so it says nothing about injectables, and no source we found sets out a full stacking matrix for med spa staff pricing. You will write that part yourself.


Three decisions are worth making explicitly:


- **Price floor, not just a percentage.** A staff rate of cost plus a fixed amount protects margin on products better than 30% off list.
- **Family members.** Decide whether the rate extends to relatives and cap the number of uses per month.
- **Provider time.** If staff treat each other during open hours, say whether that time is blocked from paying patients.


Put the staff rate in your system as its own named offer, so you can see monthly what it cost. A staff discount typed in by hand is invisible by the time you do your[KPI review](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-kpi-tracking) .


## Manager Approval for Price Overrides


Only a small named group should be able to override a price at checkout, and the reason should be recorded on the ticket. The override is where most discount leakage happens, because it bypasses every rule above.


The common pain point is the handoff. An owner described the problem to us. A manager applies a manual discount at checkout, and the front desk cannot pick up that ticket. The choices are logging out so the manager can log in, or phoning the manager and closing the sale remotely, with the patient standing at the counter. Staff who cannot apply the discount cannot finish the sale, and the manager ends up handling the checkout.


Whatever system you use, set the policy so it works in a clinic without that tooling:


1. Name the roles allowed to apply a manual discount, normally the practice manager and owner.
2. Put a dollar or percentage ceiling on what the front desk can offer without asking, such as a service recovery credit up to a small fixed amount.
3. Require a reason code or note on every override, written when the discount is given.
4. Review all overrides weekly, with the approver's name next to each one.


Role-based permissions are the mechanism. Decoda Health roles carry a separate permission for applying discounts, so a role can take payments without being able to discount. That is the same principle covered in our post on[staff roles and permissions](https://decodahealth.com/blog/decoda-calendar-permissions-staff-roles) . A one-time approval that travels with a ticket to another employee is a different capability, and Decoda Health does not offer that today.


## Birthday, Loyalty and Referral Offers Without Creating a Liability


Birthday and loyalty offers should be small, aimed at active patients and given an expiry date, because stored credit is a liability until it is spent. A $100 gift to every patient on file, including people who have not visited in two years, is the version that backfires.


A multi-service wellness clinic raised exactly this while setting up a $100 birthday points gift. They realized an automatic grant could create an unnecessary liability on the P&L, and chose to give the credit manually at first and measure how it performed. That is a good instinct. Start by hand, to patients seen in the last 12 months, and automate only after the redemption rate justifies it.


Referral rewards deserve their own page: our guide to a[med spa referral program](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-referral-program) covers when the reward is earned and how to track the referrer.


Two practical details trip people up. First, check the conversion rate if you use points: at one cent per point, a $100 gift is 10,000 points, not 100. Second, a birthday text is marketing, so it needs the patient's consent. Our post on[med spa text message consent](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-text-message-consent) covers what to collect.


Offer Who gets it Cap Expiry


Birthday credit Seen in the last 12 months $25 to $50 toward any service 30 to 60 days


Referral reward Referrer, after the new patient's first paid visit Fixed credit 90 days


Loyalty points All patients on purchases Points per dollar, redemption rate set once Set at the program level


Those figures are starting points, not benchmarks. Pick numbers your margins can carry and review them after a quarter. Because recurring plans change what a discount is worth, the notes in[VIP memberships, beauty banks and patient wallets](https://decodahealth.com/blog/setting-up-vip-memberships-beauty-banks-and-patient-wallets) are useful when deciding whether credit should be tied to a member.


## Event Promotions: Test the Rule Before the Doors Open


An event promotion behaves correctly when you write each offer as one plain sentence and then check that the rule in your system describes the same purchase. The usual failure is not the discount amount. It is a rule that fires on the wrong item.


A common version: a clinic hosts a launch event and wants "buy a package, get account credit." Two offers are meant for multi-visit packages and two for a single service bought that day and used later. If the credit rule on the second pair is attached to the service, a patient who books one ordinary treatment during the event earns a credit meant only for buyers. The owner usually notices because the redemption history looks wrong.


Before any event, define four things for every offer: what has to be in the cart (a named package, a service, or anything in a category), what the patient receives (a lower price today or credit that lands once), the two date windows (when it can be earned and when any credit can be spent), and the caps per patient, per checkout and in total. Then run three test checkouts: one that should earn the offer, one that should not, and one with a service and a package together. Read the history carefully afterward, because a log with one row per line item can look like several rewards when the patient was awarded one. Compare it with the actual credit on the account before you correct anything.


## What the FTC and HIPAA Say About Sale Prices and Birthday Offers


Two rules reach most discount programs: the FTC's guidance on price comparisons and HIPAA's marketing rule. Neither bans a discount. Both punish sloppiness in how you advertise one.


On pricing,[16 CFR 233.1](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/16/233.1) says a former price used in a comparison must be the actual, bona fide price at which the item was offered to the public on a regular basis. If your toxin price was never the crossed-out number, do not show it. Call it an event price and leave the comparison out.


On marketing,[45 CFR 164.508](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/164.508) requires written authorization to use protected health information for most marketing. A birthday message that mentions a patient's treatment history uses health information. One sent to opted-in contacts that says only "happy birthday, here is a gift from us" is far safer. State consumer-protection rules on discount advertising vary, so have counsel review your offers before launch.


## Pricing Match Offers and Third-Party Deals


If you price-match a deal-site offer, run it as a named promotion with its own rules, and do not type the markdown in by hand. Otherwise the revenue disappears into general discounts and you cannot tell whether the channel is paying for itself.


An operator in this situation told us they wanted to tag price-matched sales so a report on that channel would include them, and that the price moves around week to week. The workable pattern in most systems is a promotion that does not apply automatically, which staff add at checkout on those sales. You then report by promotion. The trade-off is that the price is variable, so decide who is allowed to set it and over what range.


Use the same discipline for any discount tied to a source. It stops one noisy offer from distorting what you think a normal ticket looks like.


## Do Discounts Hurt Your Brand?


Unplanned discounting does, because patients learn to wait for the next one. One luxury-sector critique argues that[each markdown tells clients the work was never worth the original number](https://sociallifemagazine.com/business-of-luxury/luxury-medspa-pricing/) , and that repeated cuts can fill the book while leaving margins thin.


The answer is not never discounting. It is discounting for a reason you can state in one sentence: a first visit, a membership benefit, a slow weekday. Offers like those have a clear audience and an end date. The markdown given to close one hesitant sale does not, and it is the one that spreads.


Seasonal timing matters as well. Packages sold at a discount in the fourth quarter carry undelivered balances into January, which the[seasonal cash flow guide](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-seasonal-cash-flow-planning) works through. If a discounted package is part of the offer, the terms in a[package refund policy](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-package-refund-policy) should be written first.


## Software That Enforces Your Discount Rules


The best discount policy is the one your software applies for you, so staff are not doing arithmetic at the counter. Several platforms publish what they offer. Mangomint says it can[apply discounts automatically at checkout](https://www.mangomint.com/features/offers-and-discounts.md) , and Pabau lets you set[a maximum redemption limit and start and end dates](https://pabau.com/features/offers-discounts-management-software/) for each offer.


When you compare options, ask five things: can an offer be set to apply automatically, can it be restricted by service or category, can it carry a redemption limit and end date, can you limit who may override it, and can you report by offer? The last one is the one clinics skip, and it is the one that tells you whether an offer earned its keep.

Membership discount groups can be scoped by category or by individual item, and roles can be limited so that taking payment does not include the ability to discount.

## Final Thoughts on Your Med Spa Discount Policy


Write one page. Allow one discount per ticket, name the people who can override, cap staff pricing and birthday credit, and report on every offer by name. Then review the list each quarter and drop the offers that did not pay for themselves. ## Frequently Asked Questions


Should a med spa allow discounts to stack?


Most clinics should not let discounts stack by default. Membership pricing, a seasonal promotion and a staff rate each assume they are the only reduction on the ticket, so combining them can push a treatment below cost. Write a short stacking table that names the one allowed combination, if any, and treat everything else as one discount per ticket.


What should a med spa employee discount policy include?


It should say who is eligible, which services and products are covered, the percentage or price floor, and whether it can combine with anything else. Generic templates also cap how often it can be used and exclude items already on sale. Add a line for injectables and for anything with a hard product cost, because those are where a flat percentage gets expensive.


Who should be allowed to override a price at checkout?


Give the override to a small named group, usually the practice manager and owner, and keep it away from the front desk. If a front desk employee needs an exception to close a sale, the manager approves it and records the reason on the ticket. The point is that a price change always has a person and a reason attached to it.


Are birthday discounts a good idea for a med spa?


They can work, but the offer needs a ceiling and a target. A birthday offer sent to every patient on file includes people who have not visited in two years, and any stored credit you hand them is a liability on your books. Send it to active patients, give it an expiry date and make it a small credit toward a service rather than a large cash-value gift.


How do you track which sales used a discount?


Use a named promotion for each offer instead of typing a manual markdown, then report on sales by promotion. A free-text price override tells you nothing later, while a named promotion lets you run one report and see how many sales used it and what it cost. If your software cannot tag a sale directly, a promotion that has no automatic effect and is added by staff at checkout gets you close.


Do discounts hurt a med spa's brand?


Constant, unplanned discounting can, because patients learn to wait for the next offer. Planned, limited offers with a clear reason, such as a first visit, a membership benefit or a slow weekday, do far less damage than a markdown given to close one hesitant sale. The test is whether you can explain the rule to a patient in one sentence.


Can a med spa advertise a sale price with a crossed-out regular price?


Only if the regular price is real. The FTC's pricing guides say a former price must be the actual, bona fide price offered to the public on a regular basis, and a number invented to make a discount look larger is deceptive. If a service never sold at the higher price, call the offer an introductory or event price and skip the comparison.
